say: A teacher wants to buy fruit for a class party, but she cannot ask every child one by one. How can we help her? We can make a picture graph.
Everyone chooses ONE fruit. Put your sticky dot on it. (Online: when I point to a fruit, give a thumbs up for yours. No typing needed.)
Look at the wall. Which fruit do you think won? Why do you think so?
Predict: which fruit will have the most votes and which will have the fewest? Write your guesses down.
stuck: Stuck: draw one row for each fruit first, then add the counters.
Confused about the key: “One counter stands for one child. Write it on your graph.”
For pairs who want more: ask “How many more votes did the winner get than the fruit in last place?”

say: “How many more chose green than blue? I do not add. I compare. Line up the two rows. Green has 7 and blue has 3. The difference is 7 − 3 = 4.”
“How many children voted altogether? I add all the rows: 5 + 3 + 7 = 15.”

do: Ask: “What does one picture stand for? Where does it say so?”
Ask: “Is the question asking how many altogether, or how many more? How can you tell?”
Ask: “Which row is longest? Which fruit is it? Are two fruits tied?”
stuck: Hint 2: “Point to each picture as you count it.”
Hint 3: “Draw two bars side by side and find the difference.”

say: “Would the Primary 6 pupils choose the same fruit as us?”
“What else should the teacher think about before she buys the fruit?”
ask: “Would the Primary 6 pupils choose the same fruit as us?”
Not necessarily. A class vote only tells us about our class. The teacher should also think about cost, allergies and how much fruit there is.

say: “A graph tells us about the people who voted. You noticed that, and that is a smart thing to notice.”

l3-title.note: Objective: Read and build a picture graph, compare and total data, and judge what a class vote can and cannot tell us. Materials: Sticky dots, 5 fruit pictures on the wall, counters. Online: Poll on the slide (thumbs and chat) and a shared graph the tutor builds live. Time plan: opening 0 to 2, warm-up 2 to 8 (game 2 to 6, quick questions 6 to 8; ask questions 1 to 3, and 4 and 5 only if you are on time), sneak-peek puzzles 8 to 12, explore 12 to 26, teaching 26 to 37 (click to reveal each step and answer), brain break 37 to 41, worksheet 41 to 72 with short teaching before each page and a check-together slide after it (a 30-second stand-and-stretch reset after the page-1 check, taken from that slot; the last 5 minutes check page 2, after a 1-minute stand-up stretch), talk time 72 to 79, exit ticket 79 to 85, look-back 85 to 88, then flex time and goodbye 88 to 90 (this is the buffer: if you are behind, use it; do not start anything new). Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are for every child to choose, any time or at home. Nobody is told which page they should be on.

l3-warm1.note: Minutes 2 to 6. Quick vote: each child votes for ONE fruit with a sticky dot (online: a thumbs up when the tutor points to a fruit).

l3-warm2.note: Minutes 6 to 8. Ask each question aloud, pause, then take answers. Answers: 1) From the class vote 2) From the class vote 3) From the class vote 4) Equals the number of children Ask questions 1 to 3. Ask 4 and 5 only if the clock at minute 6 is on time. The 4-minute sneak-peek puzzles follow on the next slide. Ask questions 1 to 3. Ask 4 and 5 only if the clock at minute 6 is on time. The 4-minute sneak-peek puzzles follow on the next slide. Ask questions 1 to 3. Ask 4 and 5 only if the clock at minute 6 is on time. The 4-minute sneak-peek puzzles follow on the next slide. Ask questions 1 to 3. Ask 4 and 5 only if the clock at minute 6 is on time. The 4-minute sneak-peek puzzles follow on the next slide. Ask questions 1 to 3. Ask 4 and 5 only if the clock at minute 6 is on time. The 4-minute sneak-peek puzzles follow on the next slide.

l3-warmcheck.note: Minutes 8 to 12 (4 minutes). SAY (about 26 words, once): "Two sneak-peek puzzles: ideas we have not learnt yet. A guess is a great start, and I do not know is welcome. Nobody is marked." Question 1 is an access question: every child can try it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone starts with a win. Question 2 makes you think. Children try both on their own paper (about a minute each). Then everyone answers ONCE, after the second question: face to face, each child keeps the paper low so only the tutor sees it; online, children say the answers together on three (nothing is held up to the camera). There are no private chat messages. Never use boards or paper held up in front of the group or to the camera, and never read out or compare anyone's answer. Do not write scores down or announce them. Then click to show each answer to the whole group and say "Lots of us had a different idea, and that is fine." Look for good ideas to praise in a later lesson; do not keep a list of who found question 2 easy. When the worksheet starts (minute 41) invite the WHOLE group (“When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation”), never one child by name. Everyone joins Explore and the Mini-lesson. Answers: 1) 5. Count the blue pictures. 2) 4 more (7 − 3). Compare the two rows: do not add.

l3-explore1.note: Minutes 12 to 17. Pairs work with the materials: Sticky dots, 5 fruit pictures on the wall, counters. Pairs turn the class vote into a picture graph with one counter per child, then read it aloud: most, fewest, same, how many more. Online: Poll on the slide (thumbs and chat) and a shared graph the tutor builds live. Go further (what-if) is on this slide from the start: any pair may choose it at any time, so nobody waits. The tutor does not choose who and does not announce it. Answers: Half as many pictures. The key must say 1 picture = 2 children. The winner and the total stay the same. A count that is odd needs half a picture.

l3-explore2.note: Minutes 17 to 26. Let pairs keep working and move around the room (or breakout rooms). Gather them to answer these. Answers: 1) Take away the smaller from the bigger. 2) Count in 5s, then add the rest. 3) The number of children.

l3-teach1.note: Teach. Point to the key first: "Before I count anything, I read the key. One dot stands for one child." Click 1: most, fewest, same. Click 2 and 3: how many more. Put a finger on each green dot and the blue dot above it: "This green has a partner … this one … this one. These 4 blues have no partner, so blue has 4 more." Think-aloud from the lesson script: "How many more chose blue than green? I do not add. I compare. Blue has 7 and green has 3. The difference is 7 − 3 = 4." Click 4: altogether. "I look for a 10: 7 + 3 = 10. Then 4 + 4 = 8. 10 + 8 = 18." Watch for children who add (7 + 3 = 10) when asked "how many more".

l3-try1.note: Children write on their own paper and say the answer together on three (online: nothing is held up to the camera). Never ask for boards or paper held up in front of the group or to the camera. Then click. a) Swim and cycle both have 6. b) Match up: 4 swim dots have no partner, 6 − 2 = 4. c) 6 + 6 = 12, 12 + 2 = 14, 14 + 5 = 19. For c, ask: "Did anyone find a quick way?" Anyone who answers 8 for b has added: line up the two rows again.

l3-teach2.note: Teach. Ask first: "How many children chose noodles?" Many children count the dots and say 6. Point to the key: "Each dot is 2 children." Click to step 2, then click to put the counting numbers on the dots and count in 2s together. Step 3: rice has 2 dots, so noodles has 4 extra dots; click to show them and count them in 2s: 8. Check: noodles 12 children, rice 4 children, 12 − 4 = 8. Think-aloud: "I always read the key first. One dot is 2 children, so I count in 2s, not 1s." Pizza: 2, 4, 6, 8. Total: 12 dots, count in 2s to 24.

l3-try2.note: Own paper, ticked against the answer slide. a) Count in 2s five times: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. b) Count in 3s four times: 3, 6, 9, 12. c) Count in 2s until you say 8: 2, 4, 6, 8 is 4 counts, so 4 pictures. Children can tap a finger for each count. For c, ask: "Why not 8 pictures?"

l3-teach3.note: Teach. This graph has a row missing, but we know how many children voted. Click 1: add the rows we know. Click 2: count on from 13 to 20 on fingers (7 fingers). Click 3: the rice row appears. Click 4: check. Think-aloud: "Everybody voted once, so all the rows together must make 20. Pizza and noodles make 13. How many more to make 20? I count on: 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20. Seven." Ask: "Which food won now?" (pizza, 8). Your turn (the only one in this mini-lesson after the keys of 2 and 3): children write on their own paper, then click for 5 (6 + 4 = 10, count on from 10 to 15). Take-home for children who want more (also on the Think harder slide, not for class time): the key is lost, cats have 3 pictures and 6 children chose cats (1 picture = 2 children); then dogs have 5 pictures (10 children).

l3-key.note: Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Adding when asked "how many more" (8 + 3 instead of 8 − 3). (2) Naming only one of two tied fruits. (3) Q5: missing a row when adding; tick each row as you add it. (4) Saying "Yes" in Q6 because our class chose orange. (5) Counting pictures in 1s when the key is 2 (Think harder and Go further).

l3-break.note: Four minutes. Online: children stay in view of the camera and move in place.

l3-ws1.note: Minutes 41 to 50. Pairs work together on Part A. Walk around and ask "What does one dot stand for?" and "Is the question asking how many more or how many altogether?" At minute 41 read questions 1 and 2 aloud, then pairs read the rest. The workbook says: "After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." Never announce who is on which page and never name a child in front of the group; invite the WHOLE group at once, for example: "When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Do not split a pair unless both children agree.

l3-ws1ans.note: Click each answer after a pair explains theirs. Q3: match the 3 grape dots with 3 orange dots; 5 orange dots are left. Reset (about 30 seconds, taken from this slot): when the answers are checked, everyone stands, reaches up high, shakes out their hands, takes one slow breath and sits down again, then page 2. Skip it if you are more than a minute behind.

l3-teachwho.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q6 asks if one class vote tells us about the whole school; Q7 asks what else the teacher should think about). Ask the question first and take a thumbs vote. Then click through. Ask: "How could we find out what the whole school likes?" (ask more children, every class). Step 3 ideas are only about ice cream; let children find their own ideas for fruit on the worksheet.

l3-teachtally.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Part B, where children take their own vote with tally marks). Draw a tally on the board as you say "one, two, three, four, and the fifth goes across: a bundle of 5." Click through the counting. Your turn: children count on their own paper (ticked against the answer slide), then click: 5, then 6, 7, 8. Remind them: the totals of all the rows must add up to the number of children who voted.

l3-ws2.note: Children work alone on Q6 and Q7, then the group votes together for Part B. Check that totals add up to the number of children who voted. Note who may need a short catch-up next lesson (never in front of the group).

l3-ws2ans.note: Click each answer after a child explains. Q5: one quick way is 5 + 5 = 10, 6 + 8 = 14, 10 + 14 = 24, 24 + 3 = 27. Q7: accept any sensible idea, such as cost, how many are needed, easy to share, keeps fresh, messy to eat, or a child who cannot eat it. Q8 depends on the group vote. First, everyone stands up and stretches for about a minute (reach up high, touch your toes, shake out your hands) so there is some movement before talk time.

l3-stretch.note: For any pair that chooses to try more (these are on the slide only; Think harder T1 to T4 are in the workbook). Answers: 1) 6 more. Banana 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 children; orange 2, 4 children; 10 − 4 = 6 (or: 3 extra pictures, count in 2s: 2, 4, 6). 2) Orange 7 (8 + 6 + 4 = 18, count on from 18 to 25: 7). Apple wins with 8. 3) 9. Count in 3s: 3, 6, 9, 12 is 4 pictures, so 1 picture = 3 children. Banana: 3, 6, 9. Take-home (from the Mini-lesson, not for class time): the key is lost, cats have 3 pictures and 6 children chose cats. Answer: 1 picture = 2 children (try a key of 1: 3 children is too few; try 2: 2, 4, 6). Dogs have 5 pictures: 10 children.

l3-challenge.note: For any pair that chooses Go further. Use it as a pair choice, or with volunteers in talk time (never call a child by name). Ask for the reason every time. Q3 is open: there is no single right answer, so ask children to check each other's work. Answers: 1) Banana 6 and orange 12. (24 − 6 = 18 for banana and orange; take away the extra 6: 12, share: 6 each; give orange the 6 back.) 2) 4 children (20 ÷ 2 = 10 pictures in all, counting in 2s to 20; A 3 + B 5 = 8, so C has 2 pictures = 4 children). 3) Open. Check: total 15, banana is ahead of second place by exactly 2, no ties. There are exactly two graphs: banana 7, apple 5, grape 3; or banana 8, apple 6, grape 1.

l3-chdiag.note: Show this picture slide only if a pair asks for it, or is stuck on Go further. The pictures show each problem, not its answer. Ask: What do you notice? What do we know? What do we not know yet? Can you draw or build it? Do not point out the answer; wait for a child to find a pattern.

l3-chwalk.note: Use after pairs have tried. Reveal one answer at a time and ask a child to explain before you click. Many children stop at one answer: ask "Is there another way?" and "How do you know you found them all?" For Q3, ask two pairs to swap puzzles and solve each other's.

l3-talk.note: Minutes 72 to 79. Pairs talk for 2 minutes. Then ask for volunteers first ("Who would like to share?"), never call a child by name to answer, and say that passing is always fine. No tallies and no rankings. Praise the reasons, not only the answers.

l3-exit.note: Minutes 79 to 85. Answer: 13 Extension: Draw their own picture graph from the Part B tally using one symbol per child.

l3-reflect.note: Minutes 85 to 88 (3 minutes, after the exit ticket). Children tick or write the Look-back box on the Choose and look-back page of their workbook. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out; the tutor may look at it afterwards. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby; never a direct message). Do not ask children to share their boxes. Praise the strategy ("Drawing it got you unstuck"), not the speed. The "Next time I will try" row is optional and is never marked; at the start of the next lesson the tutor may say, to the whole group, "Today you could try drawing it, using objects or checking your answer" without naming anyone. Say: "Tick what was hard and what helped you. Write or draw one thing you did well. Then tick one thing you might try next time, if you like. You can pass." After the look-back, minutes 88 to 90 are flex time: the buffer. If the lesson ran late, finish whatever is still open (stamps, the look-back). If you are on time, say goodbye and thank the parents. Do not start anything new.
